quotes.text: Directing is not about telling people what to do. It's about creating a space where truth can happen.
I don't make stories. I find them. They're already living in the world — I just give them a frame.
Bachelor Point is not just a comedy. It's a love letter to every young man who ever ate cold rice alone and called it dinner.
The best social commentary doesn't shout. It whispers — and lets that whisper echo for days.
Failure is just a first draft. The real film is still ahead.
My job is to make the audience forget they're watching a screen.
Bangladesh has extraordinary stories. We just haven't told them well enough yet.
I want to make a film that makes you call your father.

philosophy.question: What does directing mean to you?
philosophy.answer: Directing is an act of radical empathy. It means sitting with a story until you understand every character's truth — not just the hero's, but the villain's, the bystander's, the forgotten character in the background. A director without empathy is just a traffic manager.

philosophy.question: What kind of stories do you want to tell?
philosophy.answer: I want to tell Bangladeshi stories. Not the stories we imagine foreigners want to see — but the real ones. The awkward ones. The funny ones. The ones that happen in small apartments in Dhaka at 2am when no one is watching. Those stories are universal precisely because they are specific.

philosophy.question: What inspires you?
philosophy.answer: People. Always people. The way a father looks at his son when the son isn't looking. The way two strangers share an umbrella without speaking. The way the world keeps moving even when someone's heart is completely broken. These moments — they're all potential films.

philosophy.question: What is your approach to working with actors?
philosophy.answer: I give actors as much information as I can — then I get out of their way. My job in a scene is to create the conditions where something real can happen. If I'm micro-managing an actor, I've already failed. The best performances are the ones that surprise me.

philosophy.question: What is your approach to visual storytelling?
philosophy.answer: The camera should be invisible. If an audience is thinking about a beautiful shot, they've stopped thinking about the story. I only break that rule intentionally — when I want the image itself to carry a meaning that dialogue cannot. Otherwise, the camera serves the character, always.

philosophy.question: What do you want audiences to feel?
philosophy.answer: I want them to feel less alone. That is the oldest and most important function of storytelling. When someone watches my work and thinks 'that's exactly how I feel but I could never say it' — that's the moment I'm working toward.

philosophy.question: Which project changed you most?
philosophy.answer: Sorry Sir changed me. It was the first time I directed something I was genuinely afraid to make — afraid of the reaction, afraid of the consequences. The fear meant the story mattered. And the response taught me that courage in storytelling is always rewarded.

philosophy.question: What principles guide your work?
philosophy.answer: Truth first. If a scene doesn't feel true, it doesn't matter how beautiful it looks or how clever the dialogue is. Then empathy. Then courage — the willingness to tell a story even when it's uncomfortable. And finally, patience. Great art cannot be rushed.

firsts.detail: A small television drama that earned immediate critical attention for its naturalistic performance style.
Entered the nascent web series space in Bangladesh before it became mainstream.
To Let became the first Bangladeshi drama to go nationally viral on social media overnight.
Won the CJFB Performance Award for Best Director — his first major industry recognition.
Became one of the first Bangladeshi directors to create content exclusively for an OTT platform (Binge).
Bachelor Point received its first international licensing inquiry from South Asian diaspora streaming services.
